label: bm-natural-benchmarks
topic: Nature's benchmarks: pine cone, wheat awn, seed pod, Venus flytrap
summary: Natural benchmarks collected from open full texts and abstracts, with every quote re-extracted verbatim by script. PINE CONE is the only well-measured Timoshenko-type bilayer: Reyssat & Mahadevan (2009) m ~ 1, n ~ 5 (n from Dawson 1997, not read), cells ~20 percent longer wet, alpha = 0.001, response 29 min wetting and 96 min drying at 1 mm, predicted angle ~75 degrees against up to 100 observed. Eger et al (2022) measure layers of ~1.0 mm (active) and ~0.5 mm (passive), moduli 35->25 MPa (active) and 800->200 MPa (passive), +22 percent versus +1 percent length on wetting, 12-24 degree angles, 4.5 wt percent water uptake. Le Duigou & Castro (2016) give blocking forces 2.2-3.6 N and say bimetal theory fits 'fairly well' but over-predicts unless modulus is halved. My calculation (calc.py) puts these natural bilayers at 82-97 percent of the proved 3/2 ceiling from measured m and n (98-100 percent for P. pinaster only if n = 5 is assumed), never demonstrably at the exact optimum m^2 n = 1; the engineered paper/polymer strip of Reyssat & Mahadevan is at 98.8 percent. This CONTRADICTS the earlier files' adoption of m ~ 1, n ~ 5 as the pine-cone state: Eger's data give m ~ 0.5 and n = 8-23 (transverse indentation caveat). AWNS: Erodium and Pelargonium coil from tilted cellulose in a single layer (tilt 20 to 10 degrees; Erodium gruinum 46 mN, 528 uN m; Pelargonium 5.1 mN, 20.7 uN m; model within 16-25 percent for Erodium, 2.8x too high for the Pelargonium moment). Wheat awn: only the mechanism and a daily-humidity-cycle timescale; no numbers readable. PODS: Bauhinia has fibres at 45 degrees in two crossed layers and a dimensionless-width rule, but no thickness/modulus/angle values were readable (paywall); sesame capsule has an active parenchyma that shrinks to 30 percent of wet thickness with assumed stiffness ratios 20:5:0.1. FLYTRAP: closes in ~100 ms (up to 900 ms by one measure) by snap-buckling, reopens in 28-31 h; it is not a Timoshenko bilayer and is 10^4 times faster than diffusion allows at 1 mm. Theory agreement is stated qualitatively in every paper I could read; no percent error is reported except the Le Duigou modulus correction and the Ronzan model/measured ratios.
lay_summary: A pine cone opens when it dries because its scales are made of two layers that shrink by different amounts, like a strip of two metals that curls when heated. We gathered the measured sizes and speeds: the swelling layer is about a millimetre thick, the stiff layer about half that, and the scale needs roughly half an hour to an hour or two to move. A mathematical result already checked by computer says no two-layer strip can bend more than a fixed amount, and real pine cones get within about 80 to 97 percent of it, not exactly to it. Other plants do different tricks: the Venus flytrap snaps shut in a tenth of a second like a popper toy, and the cranesbill seed twists into a corkscrew from tilted threads in a single layer. Some numbers we wanted, such as those for wheat bristles and the twisting seed pod of the orchid tree, sit behind paywalls and could not be read.

findings.claim: Pine cone cell strain: single-cell ESEM shows the active-tissue cells of Pinus coulteri are about 20 percent longer wet than dry; the strain-humidity fit is eps = 0.0011*phi + 0.0033 (phi = humidity, as printed; unit of phi not stated in the caption).
findings.value: eps = 0.0011 phi + 0.0033; cells ~20 percent longer wet; alpha = 0.001 +/- 0.0001
findings.evidence_quote: The line is a linear fit to the data with equation ε = 0.0011ϕ + 0.0033.

findings.claim: Pine cone cells are about 20 percent longer in the wet state than in a dry environment (Pinus coulteri, ESEM).
findings.evidence_quote: The cells are about 20 per cent longer in the wet state (i) than in a dry environment (ii).

findings.claim: Pine cone hygroscopic expansion coefficient alpha = 0.001 +/- 0.0001 (strain per unit relative humidity) measured on single cells, said to agree with macroscopic data (Harlow 1964). Taken as per percent RH this gives 0.113 strain over 0-100 %RH (my arithmetic, calc.py), about half the '~20 percent' length change quoted for wet versus dry.

Pine cone bilayer geometry and modulus ratio used by Reyssat & Mahadevan: passive/active thickness ratio m ~ 1, active-zone length ~10 h_a, and n ~ 5 taken from Dawson et al. 1997 (the Dawson text itself could not be fetched), giving f(m,n) ~ 1.3.
findings.evidence_quote: Prior experimental measurements of the moduli of the bilayer tissues ( Dawson et al. 1997 ) suggest that n ≃ 5, so that from equation ( 2.6 ) it follows that f ( m,n ) ≃ 1.3.

findings.claim: Reyssat & Mahadevan prediction for a pine scale: curvature change ~1.3 per cm for h ~ 1 mm over zero-to-saturation humidity, angular amplitude ~75 degrees; observed scale of P. coulteri rotates by as much as 100 degrees. Predicted/observed = 0.75 using these two quoted numbers (not a like-for-like error; 100 deg is a maximum for one species).
findings.value: d_kappa ~1.3 /cm; theta ~75 deg predicted vs <=100 deg observed
findings.evidence_quote: the expected curvature change of the scale is Δκ ∼ 1.3 cm −1 (for h ∼ 1 mm and Δϕ = 100, i.e. relative humidity changing from zero to saturation)

findings.claim: Observed opening angle of a Pinus coulteri scale: up to 100 degrees when humidity of the active tissue drops from saturation to almost zero.
findings.evidence_quote: a scale from a cone of Pinus coulteri can rotate by angles as large as 100°

findings.claim: Pine scale response times scale with active-layer thickness, minutes to hours: drying tau = 96 h_a^1.5 min, wetting tau = 29 h_a^1.3 min (h_a in mm); this differs from the Washburn/diffusive h^2/D ~ 1000 s estimate at 1 mm with D ~ 1e-9 m^2/s. At h_a = 1 mm the fits give 96 min dry and 29 min wet (calc.py).
findings.value: tau_dry=96 h^1.5 min; tau_wet=29 h^1.3 min; 1 mm: 96/29 min; h^2/D=16.7 min
findings.evidence_quote: the shrinking (drying) time varies as τ d = 96 h a 1.5 min and the swelling (wetting) time varies as τ d = 29 h a 1.3 min (where h a is in mm)

findings.claim: Reyssat & Mahadevan: for strips of comparable thickness (m = 1) the curvature coefficient f changes by less than 10 percent when the modulus ratio n varies from 0.3 to 3.5.
findings.evidence_quote: for strips of comparable thicknesses ( m = 1), f ( m,n ) changes by less than 10 per cent when n varies from 0.3 to 3.5.

findings.claim: Pine cone layer thickness ratio measured by Reyssat & Mahadevan: m = h_p/h_a ~ 1 and active-zone length L_a ~ 10 h_a, roughly invariant across species (their figure 3; values read from text only).
findings.evidence_quote: the thickness ratio m = h p / h a ≃ 1, while the length of the active zone L a ≃ 10 h a

findings.claim: Reyssat & Mahadevan paper(active)/polymer(passive) strip: h_a = 100 um, h_p = 200 um (m = 2), alpha ~ 4e-4, stiffness ratio n ~ 0.4; theory gives an expected curvature change ~0.19 per mm, called 'comparable' to observation (no error number given). My f(2,0.4) = 1.48 = 98.8 percent of the 3/2 ceiling (calc.py): this engineered strip was already near the optimum.
findings.value: m=2; n=0.4; f=1.48 (98.8 % of ceiling); d_kappa~0.19 /mm; agreement 'comparable', unquantified
findings.evidence_quote: Knowing α, m and n for these devices yields an expected curvature change of about 0.19 mm −1 comparable to the experimental observations in figure 4 d

findings.claim: Pine cone tissue moduli by nanoindentation (P. wallichiana): sclereid layer 35 MPa at 50 %RH dropping to 25 MPa at 60 %RH; brown tissue 52 MPa (43 MPa at 70 %RH); sclerenchyma fibre strands fall linearly from 800 MPa (30 %RH) to 200 MPa (75 %RH). Indentation was perpendicular to the scale axis, so these are not longitudinal bending moduli.
findings.value: E_sclereid 35->25 MPa; E_fibre 800->200 MPa; E_brown 52 MPa
findings.evidence_quote: The Young's modulus of the sclereid layer (Figure 8 ) was constant at low and high humidities, but underwent an almost step‐like decrease between 50% and 60% rh, from E SC,50% = 35 MPa to E SC,60% = 25 MPa.

findings.claim: Fibre strands: modulus falls linearly on wetting from E(30%) = 800 MPa to E(75%) = 200 MPa.
findings.evidence_quote: decreased upon water uptake linearly from E SF,30% = 800 MPa to E SF,75% = 200 MPa

findings.claim: Pine scale layer thicknesses (P. wallichiana): sclereid (active) layer about 1000 um at the thickest part; sclerenchyma fibre strands (passive) constant at about 500 um. So m = h_passive/h_active ~ 0.5 here, not ~1.
findings.evidence_quote: The sclereid layer is about 1000 µm thick at the thickest part.

findings.claim: Fibre strand thickness ~500 um at the base cross-section, constant through the scale.
findings.evidence_quote: thickness of the sclerenchyma fiber strands (gray) is constant and around 500 µm

findings.claim: Dimensional change on wetting (micro-CT): sclereid layer 27 percent thicker and 22 percent longer in the bending zone; fibre strands 3 percent thinner and ~1 percent longer on the adaxial side. Differential length strain ~ 21 percent (my subtraction).
findings.evidence_quote: In the wet state, the sclereid layer was 27% thicker and 22% longer in the bending zone as compared to the dry state.

findings.claim: Scale angular change: P. sylvestris dry-to-wet (water) 24 degrees; P. wallichiana 80 to 30 %RH 12 degrees. These are two different species and humidity ranges (an earlier agent file blended them into one sentence).
findings.evidence_quote: The angular difference of the P. sylvestris scale in the dry and in the wet state is γ water = 24°

findings.claim: P. wallichiana: 12-degree angular change from 80 to 30 %RH at 23 C.
findings.evidence_quote: the P. wallichiana scale from 80% to 30% rh at 23 °C is γ 80%rh = 12°

findings.claim: Water uptake of the active (sclereid) tissue at 80 %RH is only ~4.5 wt percent, reaching equilibrium in about 20 min for small pieces. This is the mass-uptake benchmark for an engineered active layer.
findings.evidence_quote: The sclereid cells (93 mg, 23 °C, 80% rh) absorbed 4.5 wt% (≈4.2 mg water, Figure 7B ). The swelling also reached an equilibrium after about 20 min

findings.claim: Equilibration of whole scales for angle measurement was 7 h per humidity step.
findings.evidence_quote: The scales were allowed to equilibrate for 7 h.

findings.claim: Eger et al caution that the bilayer picture holds only in the basal bending zone and is 'rather simplistic regarding the whole scale'.
findings.evidence_quote: this widely accepted construction plan is rather simplistic regarding the whole scale

findings.claim: Eger et al treat the structure in the bending zone as a functional bilayer: almost no brown tissue there.
findings.evidence_quote: In the bending zone, almost no brown tissue can be found. Here, the structure can be considered as a functional bilayer

findings.claim: Pinus pinaster scales: average maximum thickness 1.3 / 1.5 / 1.1 mm (top / middle / bottom of cone) with swelling-tissue (sclerid) area fraction 65.5 / 69 / 62.5 percent. Implied m = passive/active = 0.53 / 0.45 / 0.60 (my arithmetic).
findings.evidence_quote: Average maximum thickness (mm) 1.3 1.5 1.1 Swelling tissue area (sclerids) (%) 65.5 69 62.5

findings.claim: Blocking force 3.1 +/- 0.5, 3.6 +/- 0.6, 2.2 +/- 0.1 N and blocking moment 80.5, 107.2, 42.0 N mm (top/middle/bottom).

Agreement with theory (pine cone): bimetallic-strip theory gives 'fairly good agreement' with measured blocking force but overestimates; a 50 percent reduction of dry-state Young's modulus is needed to fit, attributed to plasticisation by water. Direct support for using WET moduli in a bilayer model.
findings.value: model over-predicts; fit needs 0.5 x dry E
findings.evidence_quote: we need to take into account a 50% reduction of Young’s modulus for dry tissue to fit the experimental data with the model

findings.claim: Le Duigou & Castro abstract: fairly good agreement with bimetallic-strip theory, with overestimation.
findings.evidence_quote: A fairly good agreement is obtained when theoretical results based on bimetallic strip systems are compared with experimental data, even if overestimation is observed

findings.claim: If n = 5 (Reyssat/Dawson) holds for P. pinaster, the measured area fractions put the scale at m^2 n = 1.0 to 1.8 and f = 1.47 to 1.50, i.e. 98 to 100 percent of the 3/2 ceiling. This is my hypothesis: Le Duigou & Castro give no n; with Eger's n = 8 to 23 and m = 0.5 the same scale would sit at 82 to 97 percent.
findings.evidence_quote: Swelling tissue area (sclerids) (%) 65.5 69 62.5

findings.claim: Durability benchmark: Pinus jeffreyi scales cycled 102 times by submerging and drying kept 97 percent of blocking force and torque and over 94 percent of opening angle (about 0.03 percent force loss per cycle, my arithmetic), despite cracking and delamination.
findings.evidence_quote: they were still able to achieve 97% of their undamaged blocking force and torque and over 94% of their undamaged opening angle

findings.claim: Ulrich et al frame the work as passive facade shading, i.e. the architectural use case.
findings.evidence_quote: current architectural efforts to develop bioinspired passive façade shading systems

findings.claim: Wheat awn (Elbaum et al 2007): the abstract says cellulose-fibril arrangement bends the awns with humidity and that silicified hairs make the unit move only toward the seeds; no thickness, modulus, strain or time is in the abstract and the full text was paywalled.
findings.evidence_quote: The arrangement of cellulose fibrils causes bending of the awns with changes in humidity.

findings.claim: Wheat awn: the abstract states the awns are driven by the daily humidity cycle, so the timescale is hours (day-night), not seconds.
findings.evidence_quote: Fueled by the daily humidity cycle, the awns induce the motility required for seed dispersal.

findings.claim: Wheat-awn Young's modulus 10 +/- 2.8 GPa (ridge) to 20.5 +/- 2.6 GPa (cap) is attributed to Elbaum et al 2007 by a SECONDARY table (Mazzolai et al 2021); I could not check the primary text, so treat as unverified.
findings.evidence_quote: finding values that range from 10 ± 2.8 GPa at the ridge, to 20.5 ± 2.6 GPa at the cap

findings.claim: Awn mechanism, as summarised by Huss & Gierlinger 2021: the stress-generating layer has large or random microfibril angle, the other layer a small angle (30 degrees or less); a tilted cellulose helix makes awns coil instead of bend.
findings.evidence_quote: show a large MFA (or random orientation; Elbaum et al ., 2007 ) in the stress‐generating layer and a small MFA (≤ 30°) in the other layer

findings.claim: Erodium gruinum awn (Ronzan 2025): extensional force 45.9 +/- 22.6 mN and moment 528 +/- 54 uN m; Pelargonium appendiculatum 5.1 +/- 1.1 mN and 20.7 +/- 2.5 uN m. Model values 53.3 mN / 658.5 uN m for Erodium and 5.6 mN / 57.7 uN m for Pelargonium.
findings.value: F_ext 45.9 mN (Erodium), 5.1 mN (Pelargonium); M 528 / 20.7 uN m
findings.evidence_quote: 5.1 ± 1.1 mN and 45.9 ± 22.6 mN (5.6 mN and 53.3 mN for the model), while the moments were 20.7 ± 2.5 and 528 ± 54 µN m (57.7 and 658.5 µN m for the model)

findings.claim: Agreement with model (awns): Erodium force within 16 percent of the model (53.3 vs 45.9 mN, my arithmetic); Erodium moment model 658.5 vs measured 528 uN m (+25 percent); Pelargonium moment model 57.7 vs measured 20.7 uN m (2.8 times too high).
findings.evidence_quote: The results obtained were comparable with the model, except for the higher moment

findings.claim: Blocking forces (wet to dry): Pelargonium 0.36 +/- 0.17 mN, Erodium 6.27 +/- 1.92 mN (N = 3).
findings.evidence_quote: The blocking forces were 0.36 ± 0.17 mN and 6.27 ± 1.92 mN, respectively, for Pelargonium and Erodium

findings.claim: Erodium gruinum awn nanoindentation moduli at 50 %RH, 25 C (N = 5), inner/outer layer by region E1, E2, E3 in GPa: 0.73/0.34, 3.20/1.36, 1.73/4.17; Pelargonium P1-P3 inner/outer 1.10/2.15, 0.63/1.42, 0.55/0.94. The inner-to-outer ratio changes from region to region (not a fixed n).
Pelargonium appendiculatum awn (Cecchini 2023): cap layer 39.8 +/- 6.9 um and ridge layer 59.7 +/- 9.8 um thick (n = 6).
findings.evidence_quote: h Cap = 39.8 ± 6.9 µm and h Ridge = 59.7 ± 9.8 µm (n = 6)

findings.claim: Pelargonium awn moduli: E_cap = 0.78 +/- 0.29 GPa, E_ridge = 1.48 +/- 0.25 GPa (nanoindentation, 50 %RH, 25 C, n = 5). Read as a bilayer (my reduction): m = 1.5, n = 1.9, m^2 n = 4.3, f = 1.30 = 87 percent of ceiling.
findings.evidence_quote: E Cap = 0.78 ± 0.29 GPa and E Ridge = 1.48 ± 0.25 GPa ( n = 5)

findings.claim: Pelargonium hygroscopic expansion coefficients taken from Dawson et al as 0.20 +/- 0.04 (cap) and 0.06 +/- 0.02 (ridge). Unit is not stated; a secondary table elsewhere prints 'for dRH = 1%'. Ambiguous; do not use as a strain.

Pelargonium natural seed: torque 20.7 +/- 2.5 uN m, extensional force 5.1 +/- 1.1 mN; a 4D-printed artificial seed gave 30.4 +/- 5.1 uN m and 2.4 +/- 0.6 mN, and the authors say the theoretical model predicts the kinematics and statics within the confidence interval.
findings.evidence_quote: the developed theoretical model predicts, within the confidence interval, the kinematics and statics of the seeds

findings.claim: Erodium cicutarium awn (Evangelista 2011, via Mazzolai 2021 table): 9 +/- 2 turns, awn spiral angle 86 +/- 2 degrees, awn height 15 +/- 5 mm, maximum awn diameter 2 +/- 1 mm.
findings.evidence_quote: Number of turns: 9 ± 2 • Awn spiral angle: 86 ± 2°

findings.claim: Pelargonium appendiculatum helix at 50 %RH: radius 0.90 +/- 0.43 mm, pitch 1.85 +/- 0.24 mm, both growing with humidity (Ha et al 2020, via Mazzolai table).

Erodium coiling is NOT a two-layer Timoshenko bilayer: SAXS shows cellulose microfibrils tilted about 20 degrees at the bottom of the coiling region to about 10 degrees at the top in a single inner layer; the tilt, not a thickness/modulus ratio, sets the handedness and radius.
findings.evidence_quote: starting at about 20° tilt at the bottom of the coiling region to about 10° at its top

findings.claim: Tilted-helix awns: microfibril angle and tilt per sublayer from Abraham & Elbaum 2013 (via Mazzolai table): Erodium gruinum tilt 3, >3, 20 degrees and MFA 30, 10, 80 degrees for outermost, median, inner sublayer.
findings.evidence_quote: Erodium gruinum • Ψ = 3°, >3° and 20° • MAFH = 30, 10 and 80°

findings.claim: Bauhinia variegata pod (Armon et al 2011) abstract: pod valve turns from flat into a helix; the strip is modelled with a flat intrinsic metric and saddle-like intrinsic curvature; the authors say the theory 'quantitatively predicts all observed configurations'. No numbers (thickness, modulus, angle, time) are in the abstract; the full text was paywalled.
findings.evidence_quote: Our theoretical analysis quantitatively predicts all observed

findings.claim: Bauhinia pod valve: two fibre layers with fibres perpendicular to each other, each at 45 degrees to the long axis of the pod (as summarised in Wan et al 2018, not from Armon directly).
findings.evidence_quote: both have a 45° angle relative to the long axis of the seedpod

findings.claim: The helix of a pod strip is governed by the dimensionless width w~ = w*kappa0/t (width, intrinsic curvature, thickness), the ratio of stretching to bending energy; narrow strips twist, wide strips coil (secondary summary of Armon 2011).
findings.evidence_quote: dimensionless width w ˜ = w κ 0 / t

findings.claim: Sesame capsule (Shtein 2016): outer soft parenchyma (mesocarp) is the active layer, shrinking to 30 percent of its wet thickness on drying (they quote ~300 percent change); the stiff fibre layers barely change.
findings.evidence_quote: with the parenchyma shrinking to 30% of its wet-state thickness

findings.claim: Sesame model inputs are ASSUMED, not measured: stiffness ratios 20 (along fibres) : 5 (across fibres) : 0.1 (parenchyma) 'based on typical values from the literature'. So the passive/active modulus ratio entering the model is 50 to 200.
findings.evidence_quote: A stiffness ratio of 20 (along the fibers) to 5 (perpendicular to the fibers) to 0.1 (parenchymatous mesocarp) was selected

findings.claim: Sesame agreement with theory: a layered hygro-elastic model 'successfully simulated the opening curvature'; the curvature is written kappa_L = f*eps with f depending on stiffness anisotropy, thickness and sequence of layers (the Timoshenko structure). No error figure in text.
findings.evidence_quote: A biomechanical hygro-elastic model based on the relative thicknesses of the layers successfully simulated the opening curvature.

findings.claim: Sesame: removing the outer layer inhibited the opening movement, so the soft layer is the actuator and the fibre layers the restraint (same logic as a pine scale).
findings.evidence_quote: Removal of this outer layer inhibited the opening movement, indicating that it is the active tissue.

findings.claim: Venus flytrap (Forterre et al 2005) closes in about 100 ms; the mechanism is a snap-buckling instability whose onset the plant controls actively. Not a diffusion-limited hygromorph.
findings.evidence_quote: The rapid closure of the Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) leaf in about 100 ms is one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.

findings.claim: Flytrap snap-buckling takes 100 to 300 ms in adult traps; the lobes flip from concave to convex.
findings.evidence_quote: snap-buckling—a motion performed between 100 and 300 ms

findings.claim: Flytrap closing force 0.149 N and pressure 41 kPa between adjacent lobe rims (Volkov et al 2013, as quoted by Durak 2022).
findings.evidence_quote: closing force of 0.149 N and pressure of 41 kPa between the adjacent lobe rims

findings.claim: Flytrap seedlings close slowly: fastest seedling trap 4.96 s versus 100-300 ms for adult traps, so seedling closure is thought to be purely hydraulic and snap-buckling is acquired later.
findings.evidence_quote: The fastest snapping duration for a seedling was measured at 4.96 s

findings.claim: Flytrap closure timeline (Tsugawa 2025): the whole movement is completed within 900 milliseconds of the second stimulus; water transport takes minutes and is too slow to explain it, hence the snap-buckling hypothesis.
findings.evidence_quote: with the entire movement completed within 900 milliseconds of the second stimulus

findings.claim: Water-transport time scale in the trap is minutes, 'too slow to account entirely for the movement'; for comparison h^2/D = 1000 s at 1 mm (Reyssat & Mahadevan, D ~ 1e-9 m^2/s). Snap speed is therefore about 10^4 times faster than diffusion allows at 1 mm (1000 s / 0.1 s, my arithmetic).
findings.evidence_quote: the typical time scale of water transport is on the order of minutes, which is too slow to account entirely for the movement

findings.claim: Flytrap reopening is slow and size dependent: median 28.07 h (N clone, median trap length 23 mm) and 31.45 h (L clone, 32.72 mm); in some large traps a reverse snap-buckling stage lasts 6 to 60 min.
Reverse snap-buckling during reopening takes 6 to 60 min, far slower than closing.
findings.evidence_quote: took between 6–60 min

findings.claim: Flytrap lobe slenderness (length over thickness, simplified) median 38.67 (N) and 44.74 (L); larger, more slender traps are the ones that reopen by reverse snap-buckling.
findings.evidence_quote: median slenderness values of 38.67 and 44.74 for N and L morphotypes respectively

findings.claim: Hirata et al 2026 model the flytrap leaf as two layers: the curvature is set by the cumulative strain difference between the layers, the same quantity (delta-epsilon / h) the Timoshenko bilayer converts to curvature.
findings.evidence_quote: D can be interpreted as the cumulative effect of strain differences between the two layers translated by curvature change

findings.claim: Hirata et al 2026 abstract: closure is rapid (under 1 s); buckling, hydrostatic pressure and hydroelastic coupling have all been proposed; angular velocity correlates with a non-dimensional shape index.
findings.evidence_quote: the Venus flytrap ( Dionaea muscipula ) is known for its rapid (<1 s) trap closure

findings.claim: Aldrovanda (waterwheel plant, close relative of the flytrap): lobes 4 to 7 mm long shut in about 100 ms (Poppinga & Joyeux 2011).
findings.evidence_quote: The lobes shut in about 100 ms upon excitation of one of the 20 sensitive hairs

findings.claim: Poppinga & Joyeux's Dionaea model ASSUMES a uniform lobe thickness h = 400 um (a model input, not a measurement; the same model uses a 2 cm x 1 cm leaf).
findings.evidence_quote: We assumed uniform membrane thickness h=400

findings.claim: Poppinga & Joyeux: the fast snap of Aldrovanda comes from kinematic amplification of midrib bending, whereas Dionaea 'unambiguously relies on the buckling instability' of the two lobes.
findings.evidence_quote: the fast snapping of Aldrovanda is due to kinematic amplification of the bending deformation of the midrib

findings.claim: Poppinga & Joyeux model assumes E = 5 MPa for parenchymatous tissue as 'typical'.
findings.evidence_quote: For the Young's modulus, we used a value E=5 MPa, which is typical of parenchymatous tissues

findings.claim: Project record: the Lean file proves the Timoshenko coefficient is at most 3/(2h) for all positive h, m, n (so kappa*h/d_eps <= 3/2), with equality when m^2 n = 1. I read the file (read-only) and did not rerun Lean in this task.
findings.evidence_quote: timoshenkoCoefficient h m n ≤ 3 / (2 * h)

findings.claim: Dawson, Vincent & Rocca 1997 'How pine cones open' (Nature 390:668) resolves in Crossref; the nature.com page returned a JavaScript client challenge, PubMed has no record for the DOI, and no open full text was found. Every Dawson number in this report is therefore a secondary quotation (Reyssat & Mahadevan: n ~ 5; Cecchini: alpha 0.20 and 0.06).
findings.evidence_quote: Prior experimental measurements of the moduli of the bilayer tissues ( Dawson et al. 1997 ) suggest that n ≃ 5

findings.claim: CONTRADICTS earlier file spec-hygromorph-4d.json / spec-bilayer-physics.json (which adopt Reyssat's m ~ 1, n ~ 5 for the pine scale): the only direct tissue measurements I could read (Eger 2022, nanoindentation) give passive/active modulus ratios n = 800/35 = 22.9 (dry) down to 200/25 = 8 (wet), and thickness ratio m ~ 0.5 (500 um fibre / 1000 um sclereid). With those, m^2 n = 5.7 to 2.0 and f = 1.23 to 1.46 (82 to 97 percent of ceiling), versus f = 1.25 (83 percent) at m = 1, n = 5. Caveat: Eger indented perpendicular to the scale axis, so these are transverse, not bending, moduli.
findings.evidence_quote: E SC,50% = 35 MPa to E SC,60% = 25 MPa

findings.claim: CONFIRMS earlier spec-hygromorph-4d.json: Eger moduli (35 -> 25 MPa sclereid; 800 -> 200 MPa fibre), 1000/500 um layer thicknesses, +27/+22 percent sclereid change, 24 and 12 degree angles, and the Ulrich 102-cycle result all reproduce from the fetched texts. CORRECTS wording only: 24 degrees is P. sylvestris (water), 12 degrees is P. wallichiana (30 to 80 %RH).
findings.evidence_quote: After cyclically actuating pine cone scales by submerging and drying them for 102 cycles

findings.claim: DEEPENS earlier note on R&M alpha: alpha = 0.001 per %RH over 100 %RH gives a strain of ~0.11, about half the 'up to 20 percent' quoted for wet cells (R&M cite 'strains (up to 20%)' for wetting); the two numbers describe different wetting states (vapour vs liquid water) and R&M do not reconcile them. Eger's liquid-water mismatch (22 % vs 1 %) is closer to 20 percent.
findings.evidence_quote: The coupling of large strains (up to 20%) to water transport

findings.claim: CONFIRMS earlier spec-bilayer-physics.json: R&M's f ~ 1.3 for m ~ 1, n ~ 5 versus the project formula f(1,5) = 1.25 (about 4 percent apart; R&M round the inputs). I also checked the formula numerically on a 36-point grid: maximum f = 1.5 exactly at m^2 n = 1 and f(m,n) = f(1/m,1/n) to 2e-16 (calc.py).
findings.evidence_quote: suggest that n ≃ 5, so that from equation ( 2.6 ) it follows that f ( m,n ) ≃ 1.3.

findings.claim: DEEPENS the resin finding (project record: stock Formlabs resins gain under 1 percent mass in 24 h in water): the pine active tissue takes up only ~4.5 wt percent at 80 %RH (a vapour condition, not 24 h immersion, so the two are not like-for-like), yet its cells lengthen ~22 percent in liquid water. A bilayer therefore needs a swelling layer that converts a few wt percent of water into a large one-directional strain, and benchmarks should report strain per wt percent water, not mass gain alone.
findings.value: 4.5 wt % -> 22 % length (liquid water state differs from 80 %RH)
findings.evidence_quote: The sclereid cells (93 mg, 23 °C, 80% rh) absorbed 4.5 wt%

key_claims.claim: Measured natural pine-cone bilayers are NOT at the machine-checked optimum m^2 n = 1: Eger's tissue data (passive fibre 500 um / active sclereid 1000 um; E 800 or 200 MPa vs 35 or 25 MPa) give m^2 n = 2 to 5.7, f = 1.23 to 1.46 (82 to 97 percent of the 3/2 ceiling), and Reyssat's m ~ 1, n ~ 5 gives 83 percent. Nature sits close to, but below, the ceiling; the paper/polymer strip is at 98.8 percent.
key_claims.evidence_quote: E SC,50% = 35 MPa to E SC,60% = 25 MPa

key_claims.claim: Pine-cone benchmark numbers for an engineered bilayer to match: active layer ~1 mm and passive ~0.5 mm; differential length strain ~21 percent in liquid water (22 percent vs 1 percent), ~11 percent over 0-100 %RH by the cell-level fit; response 29 min wet / 96 min dry at 1 mm (minutes to hours); water uptake only ~4.5 wt percent at 80 %RH.
key_claims.evidence_quote: In the wet state, the sclereid layer was 27% thicker and 22% longer in the bending zone as compared to the dry state.

key_claims.claim: Timoshenko-type theory fits the natural pine cone only 'fairly well' and over-predicts unless wet (about 50 percent lower) moduli are used; the same direction as the pine fibre modulus falling 800 -> 200 MPa when wet. An engineered design must be predicted with wet-state moduli.
key_claims.evidence_quote: we need to take into account a 50% reduction of Young’s modulus for dry tissue to fit the experimental data with the model

key_claims.claim: Flytrap and Erodium are not Timoshenko bilayers: the flytrap closes in ~100 ms by snap-buckling (water transport takes minutes), and the Erodium coil comes from a single layer of tilted cellulose (20 to 10 degrees). The ceiling applies to pine cone, sesame and the paper strip; the others are analogies only.
key_claims.evidence_quote: The rapid closure of the Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) leaf in about 100 ms is one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.

glossary.plain: A material that changes shape when its moisture content changes, like a pine cone.
Two layers stuck together, one that swells and one that resists, so the strip curls.
How tightly a strip is bent: one over the radius of the circle it makes.
Thickness of the passive (restraining) layer divided by thickness of the active (swelling) layer.
How much stiffer the passive layer is than the active layer.
How stiff a material is: the force needed to stretch it, per area, per fraction stretched.
Units of stiffness or pressure: a million or a billion pascals; rubber is a few MPa, wood about 10 GPa.
How much something stretches or swells, as a fraction of its size (0.1 means 10 percent).
The proved upper limit: a two-layer strip can never bend more than 1.5 times its swelling mismatch divided by its thickness.
A quick flip from one curved shape to the opposite one, like a hair clip or a popper toy.
The direction the stiff cellulose threads in a cell wall run, relative to the cell's length.
Pressing a tiny hard tip into a surface to measure how stiff it is.
How full of water vapour the air is, as a percent of its maximum.
Percent of the dry weight that is water.
The push a bending strip makes when held in place so it cannot move.
The bristle on a grass or cranesbill seed that twists or bends with humidity.
The two kinds of woody plant cells in a pine scale: swelling ones and stiff fibre ones.
A rough time for water to soak through a layer of thickness h; grows with the square of the thickness.
A fingerprint of a file: any change to the file changes it.

recommendations: Use the pine cone as THE benchmark and state it in the proposal as numbers: active layer ~0.5-1 mm, passive layer ~0.5 mm (m ~ 0.5), length strain mismatch ~10-21 percent, water uptake ~4.5 wt percent at 80 %RH, response of minutes at 0.3-1 mm (29/96 min wet/dry at 1 mm), angular change 12-100 degrees depending on species and humidity range, and 102-cycle durability (Ulrich). Quote the ceiling as 'natural cones reach 82-97 percent of the proved 3/2 limit'.

Design to the thickness ratio, not the modulus ratio: for a measured n the optimum is m = 1/sqrt(n) (n=5: 0.447; n=8: 0.354; n=22.9: 0.209). Nature's m ~ 0.5 with n 8-23 implies pine cones are slightly thick on the passive side; an engineered strip can beat them by tuning m.

Predict with WET-state moduli. Both Le Duigou (50 percent reduction needed) and Eger (fibre 800 -> 200 MPa) show the dry-modulus model over-predicts. This supports the 'M_wet' arm already frozen in the earlier design-biomaterial.json.

Do not present the flytrap or Erodium as Timoshenko benchmarks. Use them only as analogies: flytrap = snap through (a hair clip flipping, 100 ms, 10^4 times faster than diffusion allows), Erodium = corkscrew from tilted threads, Bauhinia = a wrung towel twisting from two crossed layers, sesame = a soft cushion drying on a stiff shell, pine cone = a bimetal thermostat run by water instead of heat.

Close the gaps with a library copy: Dawson 1997 (n, alpha, units), Armon 2011 and its supplementary material (pod thickness, modulus, helix angle), Elbaum 2007 (awn modulus, bending angle). Until then keep these as second-hand and say so.

Compare engineered strain honestly: the earlier agents found stock resins and filaments swell 0.15-0.5 percent (filaments) or under 1 percent mass in 24 h (Formlabs resins). Pine active tissue changes length by 11-22 percent with ~4.5 wt percent water; the engineered bilayer should be benchmarked on strain per mass of water and on time, not only on final curvature.
